hints: Compare the three sets of reagents carefully: $\text{H}_2/\text{Pt}$, $\text{Br}_2$ with UV light, and $\text{Br}_2$ with $\text{FeBr}_3$. Think about whether each set attacks the benzene ring itself or the methyl side chain.
Recall what happens to an aromatic ring under high pressure hydrogenation with Pt, and what happens to an alkyl side chain under UV initiated bromination.
Remember that a methyl group is 2,4 directing in electrophilic substitution, so ring bromination with $\text{FeBr}_3$ gives two positional isomers.
walkthrough:
Sort out ring versus side chain attack**
Picture $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3$. You have two possible places to react: the delocalised ring and the $\text{CH}_3$ side chain. $\text{H}_2/\text{Pt}$ is powerful enough to add right across the ring and destroy aromaticity. $\text{Br}_2$ with UV light goes by radicals and attacks the side chain. $\text{Br}_2$ with $\text{FeBr}_3$ goes by electrophiles and attacks the ring.

Draw the hydrogenation and radical products**
For reaction 1, add 3 molecules of $\text{H}_2$ across the three double bonds of the Kekule form. You get a saturated cyclohexane ring still bearing the methyl group: methylcyclohexane. For reaction 2, UV splits $\text{Br}_2$ into radicals which substitute one H on the benzylic carbon. The ring is untouched, so you get $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$.

Draw the electrophilic substitution products**
For reaction 3, $\text{FeBr}_3$ generates $\text{Br}^+$ which substitutes H on the ring. Methyl is electron donating and directs ortho and para. So Br goes to the 2 position and the 4 position relative to $\text{CH}_3$. That gives two separate products: 2-bromo-methylbenzene and 4-bromo-methylbenzene.

Final answer: Reaction 1: methylcyclohexane, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}\text{CH}_3$ (fully saturated ring).
Reaction 2: (bromomethyl)benzene, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$.
Reaction 3: 2-bromomethylbenzene + 4-bromomethylbenzene (2- and 4- isomers).

hints: For reaction 1, think about what happens to the hydrogen content and the degree of unsaturation when benzene becomes cyclohexane.
For reaction 2, recall the characteristic mechanism when $\text{Br}_2$ reacts with an alkane or alkyl side chain under UV light.
walkthrough:
Name the addition of hydrogen**
In reaction 1 you are adding hydrogen across unsaturated $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bonds and removing the unsaturation. Addition of hydrogen is reduction, and for arenes it is specifically called hydrogenation.

Name the UV bromination pathway**
In reaction 2, UV light causes homolytic fission of $\text{Br}_2$ to $\text{Br}$ radicals. A benzylic H is replaced by Br through initiation, propagation and termination steps. That is the classic free radical substitution pathway.

Final answer: Reaction 1 type: hydrogenation / reduction.
Reaction 2 mechanism: free radical substitution.

hints: Think about what is preserved when H is replaced by an electrophile, compared with what is lost if the electrophile adds across a double bond in the ring.
walkthrough:
See why benzene protects its delocalisation**
Imagine breaking open the benzene ring by addition. You would use up two $\pi$ electrons to form two new sigma bonds and the continuous ring of six $\pi$ electrons would be gone. That costs a large amount of aromatic stabilisation energy. By substituting instead, the intermediate temporarily loses aromaticity but the final step restores the full delocalised ring. So substitution keeps the stable aromatic system intact and is strongly favoured.
Final answer: Substitution preserves the delocalised $\pi$ electron system / aromatic stability, whereas addition would destroy the delocalisation and lose aromatic stabilisation.

hints: Start from the standard bromination mechanism: the benzene $\pi$ system acts as nucleophile toward the positively charged electrophile, here $\text{SOBr}^+$.
Think about what the ring looks like just after the new C-S bond forms: charge, delocalisation, and which atoms carry H and $\text{S(O)Br}$.
Recall how aromaticity is restored in the second step by removal of the ring proton.
walkthrough:
Make the first C-S bond**
Let the delocalised electrons do the work. Draw a curly arrow starting inside the hexagon and pointing to the S atom of $\text{O}=\text{S}^+\text{Br}$. The pair of $\pi$ electrons forms a new C-S sigma bond. S was already positive, so it becomes neutral in the adduct.

Draw the positively charged intermediate**
Once that bond forms, the ring is no longer aromatic. Draw a cyclohexadienyl cation: positive charge delocalised in the ring, with the methyl group still attached and with both H and $\text{S(O)Br}$ attached to the same tetrahedral carbon (ortho to methyl in Fig. 5.3). This is the Wheland type intermediate.

Restore the aromatic ring**
Now remove the proton on that same carbon. Draw a curly arrow from the C-H bond back into the ring to reform the $\pi$ system, and show $\text{H}^+$ leaving. The ring becomes aromatic again, giving the 2-substituted product $\text{CH}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{S(O)Br}$ plus $\text{H}^+$.

Final answer: Curly arrow from benzene $\pi$ system to S of $\text{SOBr}^+$ to form arenium intermediate with + charge, bearing $\text{CH}_3$, H and $\text{S(O)Br}$ at the site of attack.
Curly arrow from C-H bond back into ring to reform aromatic $\pi$ system with loss of $\text{H}^+$.

hints: Count atoms: two methylbenzene units would be $\text{C}_{14}\text{H}_{16}$. Compare this with $\text{C}_{14}\text{H}_{14}\text{OS}$ to see what has been lost and what bridges the two rings.
walkthrough:
Build P from two toluene units plus SO**
Two molecules of $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3$ give $\text{C}_{14}\text{H}_{16}$. Your formula $\text{C}_{14}\text{H}_{14}\text{OS}$ has two fewer H atoms but has added $\text{OS}$ and lost $\text{Br}$. That fits a second electrophilic substitution where the $\text{S(O)Br}$ product acts as electrophile toward another methylbenzene, displacing $\text{Br}$ as $\text{HBr}$. The S=O bridge links two tolyl rings, so draw $\text{CH}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{S}(=\text{O})-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{CH}_3$.

Final answer: Diaryl sulfoxide: $\text{CH}_3\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{S}(=\text{O})\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{CH}_3$, e.g. 2-methylphenyl 2-methylphenyl sulfoxide or 2-methylphenyl 4-methylphenyl sulfoxide.

hints: Write the known $\text{SOCl}_2$ analogy: $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{SOCl}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COCl} + \text{HCl} + \text{SO}_2$, then swap Cl for Br.
walkthrough:
Copy the thionyl chloride pattern**
You already know carboxylic acid plus $\text{SOCl}_2$ gives acyl chloride plus $\text{HCl}$ plus $\text{SO}_2$. Here Br replaces Cl throughout. So $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ plus $\text{SOBr}_2$ gives ethanoyl bromide, $\text{CH}_3\text{COBr}$, plus $\text{HBr}$ plus $\text{SO}_2$. The equation is already balanced with all 1:1 stoichiometry.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{SOBr}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COBr} + \text{HBr} + \text{SO}_2$

hints: Order the three families by how electrophilic the carbon is and how good the leaving group is: acyl with Br, acyl with Cl, alkyl with Cl.
Compare C-Br with C-Cl in terms of bond strength, atomic size and orbital overlap to decide between the two acyl halides.
Compare an acyl carbon attached to $\text{C}=\text{O}$ with an alkyl carbon attached to electron donating R groups to decide why alkyl chlorides are slowest.
walkthrough:
State the order**
Think of hydrolysis as water attacking a $\delta+$ carbon and displacing $\text{X}^-$. The more $\delta+$ the carbon and the weaker the C-X bond, the faster it goes. That gives $\text{RCOBr}$ fastest, then $\text{RCOCl}$, then $\text{RCl}$ slowest.

Explain acyl bromide versus acyl chloride**
Focus on the leaving bond. Br is larger than Cl, so the $\text{C}(2p)$ to $\text{Br}(4p)$ overlap is much poorer than $\text{C}(2p)$ to $\text{Cl}(3p)$ overlap. The C-Br bond is therefore longer and weaker and breaks more easily on attack by water, so acyl bromides hydrolyse most readily.

Explain acyl versus alkyl**
Now look at the carbon. In $\text{RCOX}$ the carbon is joined to two electronegative atoms, O and X, and the $\text{C}=\text{O}$ group strongly withdraws electrons. The carbonyl carbon is highly $\delta+$ and very attractive to nucleophiles, and the C-X bond is weakened. In $\text{RCl}$ there is no $\text{C}=\text{O}$, and alkyl groups push electrons toward carbon by the positive inductive effect. That reduces the $\delta+$ charge and strengthens the C-Cl bond, so alkyl chlorides hydrolyse slowest.

Final answer: Easiest to hydrolyse: acyl bromides, $\text{RCOBr}$ > acyl chlorides, $\text{RCOCl}$ > alkyl chlorides, $\text{RCl}$ : hardest to hydrolyse.
Acyl bromides easiest as C-Br is much weaker than C-Cl due to poorer orbital overlap / larger Br atom.
Acyl halides easier than alkyl chlorides as carbonyl C is more $\delta+$ / electron deficient due to electron withdrawing $\text{C}=\text{O}$ and C-X bond is weaker; alkyl chlorides hardest as C-Cl is strengthened by positive inductive / electron donating effect of alkyl groups.
